title: Pine
description: Pine is the most common softwood for general carpentry: light, soft, inexpensive, and easy to cut, nail, and glue. Its grain is straight with prominent darker growth rings and occasional knots, and it takes stain unevenly unless a pre-stain conditioner is used first. Eastern white pine is softer and clearer than yellow pine, which is denser and stronger and suits structural work. Pine moves noticeably with humidity, so interior pine should be acclimated in the room for several days before it is cut. Pine dust is a respiratory irritant, so sanding calls for a dust mask and extraction.

Inspect each board for knots, splits, and twist, and mark the best face.
Cut test pieces and check how the stain or paint behaves on an offcut.
Apply pre-stain conditioner if staining, then stain or paint as planned.
Let the finish cure fully before stacking boards face to face.

N=3

print('Boards: ' + str(N) + ', total board feet: %.2f' % tot)
print('Cost at $%.2f per board foot: $%.2f' % (PRICE, tot*PRICE))

Board feet per board: 6.00

title: Oak
description: Oak is a strong, open-grained hardwood in two main kinds: red oak, which is pinkish-brown and porous, and white oak, which is browner, denser, and more water-resistant. Its prominent grain and ray fleck make it a classic furniture and flooring wood, and it holds screws and joints exceptionally well. Red oak's open pores drink up finish and need grain filler for a smooth top, while white oak suits outdoor use better because its pores are plugged with tyloses. Oak dust is a strong irritant, so sand with a mask and good extraction, and avoid iron fasteners in wet oak, which stains the wood black.

title: Maple
description: Maple is a pale, dense hardwood with a fine, even grain that finishes beautifully and resists dents, which is why it is the standard wood for butcher blocks, workbench tops, and cutting boards. Hard maple is much denser than soft maple, and figured maple with curl or birdseye commands a premium for visible panels. Maple burns easily under dull router bits and saw blades, so sharp tooling and steady feed matter, and it can blotch under stain, so a conditioner or a gel stain gives a more even color. Maple dust calls for a mask, and maple glue joints are among the strongest in woodworking when the surfaces are fresh and flat.

title: Walnut
description: Walnut is a dark chocolate-brown hardwood prized for fine furniture, and its color varies from pale sapwood at the edge to deep heartwood in the center. It machines, glues, and finishes superbly, and a simple oil finish brings out a depth that few other woods match. Walnut is expensive, so careful layout matters: plan cuts to keep sapwood out of visible faces, or steam the sapwood color in where a uniform look is wanted. Walnut dust can irritate skin and lungs, so wear a mask and gloves when sanding, and keep walnut shavings away from horses, for which they are toxic.

title: Cherry
description: Cherry is a warm reddish-brown hardwood that darkens with age and light exposure, so a new cherry piece will deepen in color over its first months in a sunny room. Its grain is fine and straight with occasional gum pockets, and it finishes to a smooth, glowing surface with oil or lacquer. Cherry burns readily under dull tools, so sharp blades and steady feed are essential, and it blotches under stain unless a conditioner is used. Because cherry darkens unevenly, keep finished pieces out of patchy sunlight and let the whole piece age evenly.

title: Poplar
description: Poplar is a light, soft hardwood that is the workhorse of painted projects: it is inexpensive, stable, easy to machine, and paints to a smooth surface with no visible grain telegraphing through. Its natural color runs from pale cream to greenish-brown streaks, which is why it is rarely used for clear finishes, though the green tones fade with light. Poplar takes screws and glue well, dents more easily than oak or maple, and is an ideal first hardwood for learning joinery. Poplar dust still calls for a mask, as with all wood dust.

title: Cedar
description: Cedar is a light, aromatic softwood that resists rot and insects naturally, which makes it the standard wood for outdoor furniture, decking, and closets. Western red cedar is soft, straight-grained, and weathers to a silver-grey if left unfinished, while aromatic red cedar's strong scent repels moths in closets and chests. Cedar splits easily, so screws near ends must be pre-drilled, and its softness means it dents under heavy use. Cedar dust can irritate lungs and skin, so sand outdoors or with extraction and a mask, and never burn cedar scraps in a closed stove without checking local rules, since the oils smoke heavily.

title: Plywood
description: Plywood is made of thin wood veneers glued with their grain directions alternating, which makes a sheet that is strong, flat, and far more stable than solid wood of the same size. Grades run from cabinet-grade birch and maple plywood with clean faces down to construction CDX with knots and patches, and the right grade depends on whether the face will show. Plywood cuts best with a fine-tooth blade and a scoring pass or tape on the cut line to prevent tear-out on the face. Plywood dust and the adhesives in it call for a mask, and formaldehyde-free options exist for interior cabinetry.

title: MDF
description: MDF, medium-density fiberboard, is made of wood fibers pressed with resin into a dense, perfectly flat sheet with no grain, which makes it ideal for painted panels, routed profiles, and speaker boxes. It machines beautifully and takes paint to a glass-smooth surface, but it is heavy, it swells and falls apart if it gets wet, and its edges soak up paint unless sealed first. MDF dust is fine and heavy and must be controlled with extraction and a respirator, and screws need pilot holes and coarse threads or they will strip. MDF is never used where it will stay wet, and it is never used for structural spans without support.

title: OSB
description: OSB, oriented strand board, is made of wood strands pressed in layers with their directions alternating, and it is the standard structural sheathing for walls, floors, and roofs. It is strong and inexpensive, though its rough surface is never used as a finished face, and its edges swell if they stay wet for long. OSB panels carry span ratings stamped on the sheet, and those ratings must be followed for floors and roofs. OSB dust calls for a mask, and OSB offcuts are not used for fine furniture, since the surface cannot be finished smooth.

title: Particleboard
description: Particleboard is made of wood particles pressed with resin into a flat, inexpensive sheet, and it is the core of most low-cost shelving and flat-pack furniture, usually covered with melamine or veneer. It is weaker than plywood or MDF, it sags under load at long spans, it swells badly when wet, and screws strip easily unless special particleboard screws or inserts are used. Its one virtue is price and a perfectly flat face for laminate. Particleboard dust calls for a mask, and particleboard shelves must be kept short, supported, and dry.

title: Hardwood Veneer
description: Hardwood veneer is a thin slice of real wood, typically 1/42 inch thick for commercial veneer, glued onto a stable substrate such as MDF or plywood to give the look of solid hardwood at lower cost and with better stability. Book-matching, where consecutive slices are opened like a book, creates symmetrical grain patterns that are the hallmark of fine cabinetry. Veneer work demands clean glue surfaces, even pressure from a veneer press or vacuum bag, and careful trimming, because veneer tears and bubbles easily. Veneer dust and contact cement fumes both call for ventilation and a mask.

title: Reclaimed Lumber
description: Reclaimed lumber is wood salvaged from old barns, factories, and buildings, and it carries nail holes, weathering, and a patina that new wood cannot imitate. It must be inspected with a metal detector and denailed before any machine touches it, because a hidden nail destroys planer knives and can throw dangerous fragments. Reclaimed boards are often old-growth wood, denser and more stable than new lumber of the same species, but they vary in thickness and need jointing and planing to a uniform size. Reclaimed lumber may carry old paint, including lead paint on pre-1978 buildings, so test painted boards and never sand suspected lead paint without proper precautions.

title: Bamboo Plywood
description: Bamboo plywood is made of bamboo strips laminated into sheets, and it is harder than most hardwoods, with a distinctive striped grain that reads as modern and clean. Bamboo grows far faster than trees, which makes it a renewable choice, and its hardness suits flooring, cutting boards, and countertops. Bamboo dulls cutting tools faster than pine, so carbide tooling is recommended, and its glue lines can be hard on saw blades. Bamboo dust calls for a mask, and bamboo plywood should be finished with oil or polyurethane to keep its color from fading in sunlight.

title: Pressure-Treated Lumber
description: Pressure-treated lumber is pine or fir forced full of preservative under pressure so it resists rot and insects in ground contact and outdoor use, and it is the standard wood for decks, fences, and posts. Modern treatments are copper-based and far less toxic than the old chromated copper arsenate, but treated lumber is still not used for cutting boards, food contact, or indoor furniture, and its dust and offcuts are never burned. Treated lumber arrives wet and heavy and shrinks as it dries, so deck boards are installed tight and allowed to gap as they dry, and only hot-dipped galvanized or stainless fasteners are used, because standard steel corrodes in contact with the treatment chemicals.

title: Lumber Grading and Selection
description: Lumber grading is the system that sorts boards by strength and appearance, and knowing it saves money and prevents failures. Hardwood lumber is graded by the percentage of clear, defect-free wood in the board, from FAS at 83 percent clear down to Number 1 Common at 66 percent, while softwood dimension lumber is graded by strength, with Select Structural at the top and Number 2 as the common framing grade. Moisture content matters as much as grade: interior lumber should measure 6 to 8 percent, exterior lumber 12 to 15 percent, and a simple pin meter checks it in seconds. Selecting lumber means sighting down each board for bow, cup, twist, and crook, rejecting boards with splits at the ends, and buying boards a little longer than needed so defects can be cut away.

specs.dimensions: Hardwood grading: FAS 83 percent clear, Number 1 Common 66 percent clear; softwood: Select Structural, Number 1, Number 2
details: FAS clear yield: at least 83 percent
Number 1 Common clear yield: at least 66 percent
Interior moisture target: 6 to 8 percent
Exterior moisture target: 12 to 15 percent
Reject twist over 1/4 in in an 8 ft board for fine work
Cost tier: grade decides price; FAS costs roughly twice Number 1 Common
fasteners: No fasteners in the material guide itself
specs.tolerances: Board dimensions within 1/32 inch; moisture content 6 to 8 percent for interior work
specs.arithmetic_note: Movement checks out: width times coefficient times moisture-change percent. Demo output below was captured by executing the demo code at build time.

steps: Measure moisture with a pin meter before buying.
Sight down every board for bow, cup, twist, and crook.
Check the grade stamp or ask the supplier for the grade.
Buy boards 6 to 12 inches longer than the finished length.
Sort boards at home by color and grain before cutting.

required: Hand plane or sander for test pieces
tools.safety_notes: Wear a dust mask when sanding and cutting, and use dust extraction where available. Check every board for nails or staples before machining.

demo.code:
W=12
COEF=0.003
MC=6
move=W*COEF*MC
print('Board width: ' + str(W) + ' in, movement coefficient: ' + str(COEF) + ' per inch per percent moisture change')
print('Moisture change: ' + str(MC) + ' percent')
print('Expected movement across the width: %.3f in' % move)
print('Allow at least %.2f in of clearance for this movement' % (move+0.03))
